# My van almost caught fire. Here's what went wrong, and what to check on yours.

This isn't the post I wanted to write. I'd rather be posting before-and-afters of a doodle who finally let me do her feet. But I need to write this one, mostly for Tasha, and for the rest of you who groom out of a van with a big inverter setup and assume it's fine because it looks fine. I did too.

First, everyone is okay. Me, the client, and the dog. The van is not okay, and I'm off the road for at least three weeks. I'll get to all of it.

**I'm not an electrician.** I groom dogs. Everything technical in here is what Priya, the marine electrician who's fixing my van, explained and showed me, and I've tried hard to get the numbers right. Please don't use this post as wiring instructions. Use it to figure out what questions to ask and when to call a professional.

## What happened

Wednesday, October 28, around 2:15 in the afternoon. I was in a client's driveway in Bedford drying Moose, a Bernese and a very good boy, on high. If you've dried a Berner you know that's a long time at full blast.

I smelled hot plastic first and figured it was the dryer motor. Dryers smell weird sometimes, especially working that hard, so I kept going for a bit. Then I saw smoke coming out of the bench seat, which is where my batteries live.

I don't fully remember deciding to do anything. I killed the battery switch, opened the side door, and got Moose out, still damp. He was thrilled, honestly. Best part of his day. Then I grabbed the extinguisher and gave the battery area a spray. I'm still not sure I needed to, because once the power was off the smoke started dying down, but I wasn't going to stand there and find out.

When I could look properly, the lug on the positive cable going into the inverter was black, and the jacket on the cable had melted back about 3 cm from the end.

Moose's mom came out with a coffee and sat with me on her front steps while I shook. I'll never forget that. If you're reading this, thank you.

## My setup

So you can compare to your own van:

- 3000W inverter
- Two 200Ah lithium batteries, 12V system
- Built by Coastline Van Fitouts (Darren) in spring 2025

It looked really tidy. Cables zip-tied in neat runs, everything labelled, heat-shrink on all the ends. That's a big part of why I trusted it. I've had a lot of time to think about this over the last couple of weeks, and the main thing I'd tell anyone is that **tidy is not the same as right.**

## What was actually wrong

I took the van to Priya at Sackville Marine Electric. She went through everything and found three main problems, plus one I'd missed completely. I'll explain each one the way she explained it to me.

### 1. The cable was way too small

The cable from my battery to my inverter was **4 AWG**. Priya says for a 3000W inverter on a 12V system it should have been at least **2/0** (say "two-aught"). Quick note, because this tripped me up: with these cable sizes, a *bigger* number means a *thinner* cable. 4 AWG is a lot thinner than 2/0. She showed me the two side by side and the difference was obvious. 2/0 is a much fatter cable.

Here's why it matters. Electrical power is volts times amps. At 12 volts you need a lot of amps to make a lot of watts, and amps are what heat up a cable.

- My dryer pulls around 1800 to 2000W. At 12V, 2000W works out to about 167 amps. Inverters also lose some power as heat while they convert, so the batteries are really supplying a bit more than that.
- Sometimes the water heater is running at the same time, which pushes it up toward 250 amps.
- A 3000W inverter running flat out at 12V can pull roughly 250 to 300 amps from the batteries.

A 4 AWG cable isn't built to carry that kind of current for long. Priya's comparison was trying to drain a bathtub through a drinking straw. It *works*, but everything gets hot and stressed. Every time I dried a big dog on high, that cable was cooking a little. Moose just happened to be the day it got too far.

The worst part is that I dried big dogs on that setup for months. It didn't fail the first day. It got worse slowly, which is exactly why nobody noticed.

### 2. The crimp on the end was bad

This was the spot that actually burned.

The big copper ends on battery cables, the round metal bit with a hole that bolts onto a terminal, are called **lugs**. A lug needs to be crimped onto the cable with a proper hydraulic or heavy-duty crimper. That squeezes the lug and cable together so hard they're basically one solid piece of metal.

The lug on my positive cable looked like it had been crimped with pliers, or possibly hammered. Priya could tell from the shape once she cut the heat-shrink off. The heat-shrink had been covering it the whole time, so from the outside it looked perfect.

A bad crimp means a loose connection inside, and a loose connection means resistance. Resistance plus a couple hundred amps means heat, all concentrated right at that one spot. Combine that with a cable that was already too small and running hot, and that lug was the weakest point in the whole system. That's where it went.

### 3. The fuse wouldn't have saved me, and it was in the wrong place

I had a **300A ANL fuse**. I'd always thought "great, I have a fuse, so if anything goes wrong it'll blow." Priya explained why that wasn't true in my case, and this part honestly scared me the most.

**Problem one: the fuse was too big for the cable.** A fuse is there to protect the *wire*. It's supposed to blow before the cable gets dangerous. My fuse was rated 300A, but my 4 AWG cable couldn't safely handle anywhere near 300A. So the cable could overheat and melt at, say, 200 amps, and the fuse would just sit there happily, because 200 is less than 300. The fuse and the cable didn't match. That's a design problem, not bad luck.

Also, what happened to me wasn't a short circuit. It was a cable slowly overheating under normal load. A fuse only blows when the current goes over its rating, and mine never did. It was never going to blow.

**Problem two: it was too far from the battery.** My fuse was mounted about **90 cm** from the battery. Priya says it should be within roughly **18 cm**. The fuse only protects the cable *after* it. Everything between the battery and the fuse is unprotected, and in my van that was almost a metre of cable with nothing guarding it.

**Problem three: wrong type of fuse for lithium.** This one I'd never heard of. Lithium batteries can dump a massive amount of current very fast if something shorts. ANL fuses aren't rated to safely interrupt that much. Priya is putting in a **Class T fuse**, which is built for exactly this. She was pretty firm that if you have big lithium batteries, a Class T should be in there close to the battery.

### 4. No smoke detector in the back

The only smoke detector in my van was the one in the cab that came with it. Nothing in the back near the batteries, inverter, or dryer, which is where the fire risk actually is. I was standing right there so I caught it, but if this had happened while I was inside a client's house collecting a dog, or between appointments, nothing would have warned me.

## The part that really got me

Priya has a van too, running a similar kind of load. She pulled up thermal camera pictures of her own setup while it was running, the kind where hot spots show up bright orange and cool stuff is blue and purple. Then she put my damage photos next to them.

Her cables and lugs were barely warm, just a little colour. Mine was a burnt black lug and a melted jacket. Same kind of job, same kind of power, completely different result, and the only difference was how it was built.

That's when it really sank in that this wasn't a freak accident. It was predictable, and someone who knew what they were looking at could have caught it in about ten minutes.

## About Darren

I want to be careful here. I'm not trying to trash anyone publicly. I'm going to state the facts and you can make up your own minds.

- Coastline Van Fitouts did my electrical in spring 2025.
- The cable size, crimp, fuse size, fuse location and fuse type are what a licensed marine electrician found and documented.
- I've reached out to Darren three times by text and once by email since the incident. I haven't heard back yet.

If he gets back to me I'll update this. That's all I've got to say about it.

## Tasha, this part is for you

Tasha, I know you're about to put a deposit down with the same builder. I'm not telling you what to do. But before you pay anything to *anyone*, please get these in writing:

1. **Cable size** for the main battery-to-inverter runs, the actual gauge, and what inverter size it's for.
2. **Fuse type and rating** on the main battery line, and whether it's matched to that cable.
3. **Where the main fuse will be mounted**, and how far from the battery.
4. **Whether they're using a Class T fuse** with lithium batteries.
5. **What tool they crimp lugs with.** You want a hydraulic crimper or a proper heavy-duty lug crimper. Not pliers, not a hammer crimper.
6. **Whether there'll be a smoke detector in the back** near the electrical.

Any good builder will happily answer these and write them down. If someone gets cagey or says "don't worry about it," that tells you something.

Then honestly, once it's built, pay an independent electrician to look it over before you start working out of it. It'll cost way less than what I'm about to pay.

This goes for all of you groomer girls, not just Tasha. Our setups pull way more power than most campervans. Hair dryers and water heaters are basically the worst-case load, running hard for a long time, every single day.

## A checklist you can do on your own van

Again: **I'm not an electrician.** This isn't a substitute for a pro. It's a way to spot obvious red flags so you know whether to book someone. If anything on this list looks wrong, stop using the inverter for heavy loads and get it looked at.

**Do this with everything OFF.** Turn off the inverter, turn off the battery switch, and unplug any shore power or solar. Don't take anything apart. Just look and touch the outside of cables.

**Cable size**
- [ ] Find the big cables from your batteries to your inverter. The size is usually printed on the jacket in tiny letters, something like "4 AWG" or "2/0." You might need your phone flashlight.
- [ ] Write down what you find, along with your inverter's wattage and whether you're 12V, 24V or 48V. Bring that to an electrician and ask if it matches. For reference, mine was 4 AWG on 3000W at 12V, and Priya said it needed 2/0 minimum.

**Fuse**
- [ ] Find your main fuse on the positive cable coming off the battery. It's usually in a black box or holder.
- [ ] Measure roughly how far it is from the battery terminal along the cable. Priya says within about 18 cm.
- [ ] Note the rating (the number on it) and the type. ANL fuses are flat with bolt holes on each end. Class T fuses are more cylinder-shaped. If you have lithium batteries and no Class T, ask an electrician about it.
- [ ] Ask a pro whether your fuse rating actually matches your cable size. A big fuse on a small cable is what I had.

**Lugs and connections**
- [ ] Look at every lug on the main cables. Any discolouration? Brown, blue, black or rainbow-tinted metal can mean it's been getting hot.
- [ ] Look at the heat-shrink and cable jacket right where they meet the lug. Melted, shrunken back, bubbled, shiny or crispy is bad.
- [ ] With the power OFF, give each cable a gentle tug right at the lug. It should feel totally solid. If it wiggles or turns inside the lug, that's a problem.
- [ ] If you can see the crimp, a good one usually has a neat hex shape or a clean deep dent. A flattened, squished or uneven look is a red flag.
- [ ] Sniff. Seriously. Any hot plastic or burnt smell around the battery area, even faint, get it checked.

**General**
- [ ] Are cables secured so they can't rub or bounce around when you drive?
- [ ] Where cables pass through metal, is there a rubber grommet or some protection so the edge can't cut into them?
- [ ] Is there a smoke detector in the back near the batteries and inverter? If not, buy one today. They're cheap.
- [ ] Do you have a fire extinguisher you can actually reach in a hurry, rated for electrical fires? Check the gauge too.
- [ ] Do you know exactly where your battery shut-off switch is, and can you hit it without thinking? Mine is the reason this ended the way it did.

### The cheap tool everyone should own

Get an **infrared thermometer**, the kind you point and click and it reads the temperature of whatever you're aiming at. I got mine for about 40 bucks at Canadian Tire.

This is the one check you do with the power **on**, and **you never touch anything**, you just point it from a distance.

- Run your normal heavy load, like your dryer on high, for 10 to 15 minutes.
- Point the thermometer at each lug and connection on your main cables, plus the cable itself, the fuse, and the inverter terminals. Keep your hands away.
- You're comparing. Everything should be roughly similar and only a bit warm. If one connection reads noticeably hotter than the others, that's your problem spot. It's exactly what my bad lug would have shown.
- If anything reads hot, turn it all off and get an electrician in.

I keep thinking that if I'd owned one of these and spent five minutes checking once a month, I'd have seen that lug heating up long before it burned.

## Where I'm at right now

I'm going to be honest, because that's kind of the point of this blog.

**The repair.** The quote is $4,200. Priya is redoing the main cable runs with properly sized cable and proper crimps, putting in a new fuse block, and adding a Class T fuse in the right spot near the batteries. It's at least three weeks, because some parts are on order.

**The money.** I've cancelled 31 appointments so far, and that number is still going up. My insurance says "maybe." The adjuster is coming Thursday, and I'll update you when I know more.

**Me.** I'm scared, honestly. That van is my entire income. Rent is due on the 1st, and I'm doing a lot of math at 2am that doesn't add up the way I want it to. I'm trying to remember that a damp Bernese and a shaky groomer on someone's front steps is the *good* version of this story. It could have been a lot worse, and I'm really grateful it wasn't.

To all my clients who've been rescheduled, thank you for being so kind about it. I've had so many nice messages and I'm sorry I'm slow answering them. I'll be back on the road as soon as the van is safe, and only once it's safe.

I'll post again when the van is back, with photos of the new setup and hopefully some thermal pictures of my own that look as boring as Priya's.

Until then, please go look at your batteries. Bring a flashlight, take five minutes, and if anything looks off, call someone who knows what they're doing.

And give your dogs a squeeze for me. Moose already got his.
